newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia, Europe pick through minefield to forge ties.
newsitem.headline: Asia, Europe pick through minefield to forge ties.

text.p: Burma, East Timor and other human rights issues hung like thunderclouds over major meetings between Asia and Europe on Wednesday aimed at forging a new era of relations.

Foreign ministers of the seven-nation Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) insisted that such issues not be raised in meetings with their 15 European Union counterparts on Thursday and Friday.

Indonesia threatened to walk out if East Timor was brought up at those meetings or on Saturday, when the 22 ministers will be joined by colleagues from Japan, China and South Korea to plan a second Asia-Europe summit.

But European politicians facing pressures back home, especially on the crackdown on Burma's pro-democracy movement by the military government in Rangoon, were seeking ways to discuss such issues without bringing the meetings to a crashing halt.
"At the back of everyone's mind -- actually at the front -- are human rights, labour rights and Burma," said one EU official in Brussels.
"How do you speak about the unspeakable? These subjects have to be raised, yet no one wants to be the one to do it."

Burma is an issue because ASEAN -- Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam -- has promised membership to Rangoon along with Laos and Cambodia. The question is only when this will happen.
The European Parliament has repeatedly warned the European Commission -- the group's executive -- that it will not tolerate dealings with Rangoon.

Along with what Europe sees as an Asia teeming with sweat shops taking European jobs, and East Timor -- seized by Indonesia more than 20 years ago when EU member Portugal gave up control -- Burma is a potential conference wrecker.
But ASEAN officials say they expect the ministers to pick their way through this minefield of sensitive issues as their leaders did a year ago in Bangkok, when the first Asia-Europe summit was held.

Then, East Timor was the potential bomb with Portugal and Indonesia in attendance. The leaders of the two countries met privately on the sidelines to discuss an issue on which they are radically opposed, and the conference was unhindered.
ASEAN officials said they hoped the Burma issue could be defused as easily this year in Singapore.

"We will not allow one or two difficult issues to distract our attention from the positive agenda," said one. "My hope is that we can take stock of what we have achieved up to now and also review the potential of greater things to come.

"I am just hoping that officials and ministers on both sides will see that there is tremendous potential for a positive agenda, and not allow our different perspectives to wreck the meeting," said the official, who declined to be identified.
At issue is a grand vision of a radical transformation of relations between Asian and European nations, several of which have been major colonial powers in the region.
Last year's Bangkok summit set out an ambitious agenda, ranging from closer economic ties to linking the rail systems of the two regions.

Since then, senior economic officials have met to talk trade and investment, and business leaders have discussed how to improve contacts between the private sectors of the old economic powerhouse and the new.
Economic and finance ministers are due to meet this year, ahead of the second Asia-Europe summit scheduled to be held in Britain next year.
